title: The History of Jersey Club Music, From Newark to the World
description: How Jersey club music started in Newark around 1999, who built it, and how the Brick Bandits turned a local party sound into a global genre.
dek: Before the TikTok dances and major-label remixes, Jersey club was burned onto CDs and sold on the streets of Newark. This is how it started and who built it.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Every track on this station can be traced back to a small group of Newark DJs working around 1999 and 2000. [DJ Tameil](/artists/djtameil) and Tim Dolla were making what they called Brick City club music. It was faster and harder than the Baltimore club records that were already filling dance floors along the East Coast, and it belonged to Newark.

Tameil was one of the first to produce his own tracks. He put out the Dat Butt EP on his label, Anthrax Records, and sold burned CDs on Broad Street. With Mike V and DJ Black Mic he became part of the Brick Bandits, the crew that did the most to establish the sound in those early years.

You know it within a bar or two. The tempo sits around 130 to 140 BPM. The kicks land in hard triplet patterns, vocal clips get chopped into hooks, and there is usually a bed squeak lifted from Trillville's "Some Cut." Baltimore gave it the bounce. New Jersey gave it history, since the state was already house music country, home to Kerri Chandler, Tony Humphries and the legendary Newark club Zanzibar.

body.h2: From small rooms to the internet

body.p: The scene grew in places like The Life Lab, where younger Brick Bandits members threw a party called THREAD. Then it moved online through MySpace, SoundCloud and mix CDs passed from hand to hand. [DJ Lilman](/artists/djlilman) and DJ Frosty made tutorial tracks and videos that taught a generation how to dance to it. When [DJ Sliink](/artists/djsliink) remixed Trey Songz's "Na Na" for Atlantic Records, the major labels were paying attention.

body.quote: Jersey club is your morning coffee and your midnight Red Bull.
body.by: UNiiQU3, speaking to The FADER in 2014

body.p: That still holds up. There are far more producers now and the tempos keep climbing, but the formula from Broad Street is audible in every track on this week's [Rising Now chart](/hot). For the story of how the sound broke out online, read [how TikTok turned Jersey club into a global sound](/news/how-tiktok-made-jersey-club-go-viral).

title: How TikTok Turned Jersey Club Into a Global Sound
description: Jersey club took over TikTok in 2022, but its dances were spreading on Vine and Musical.ly years earlier. Here is how the Newark sound went viral.
dek: Jersey club felt brand new to a lot of people on TikTok in 2022. The dances and the sound had been traveling online for years before that.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: When Jersey club seemed to be on every For You page in 2022, plenty of people assumed it was a new trend. It had been growing in Newark since the early 2000s, and its dances were already moving through Vine and Musical.ly between 2014 and 2018.
Some of the moves that went viral are older than the apps. [DJ Lilman](/artists/djlilman)'s 2011 track "I Like The Way She Move" introduced dance moves that came back years later as TikTok trends.

body.h2: Why the beat works in a 15-second clip

body.p: A lot of it comes down to structure. The bouncing kick patterns and signature sounds, like the bed squeak and the five-count kick, are easy to recognize within a few seconds of video. The same elements have since shown up on mainstream records, including Drake's "Massive."
The sound opened doors for rappers too. Newark's Bandmanrill built his career rapping over Jersey club production.

body.quote: I only started rapping over Jersey Club beats because I wanted to be different.

body.p: At home, collectives like Project X, a Jersey crew of producers, dancers and artists, kept the culture rooted in the city while the rest of the world caught up.

body.h2: The song that broke it open

body.p: The biggest moment came in October 2022 with Lil Uzi Vert's "Just Wanna Rock," co-produced by 19-year-old Newark producer MCVertt. We cover that record in detail in [how MCVertt's beat took Jersey club mainstream](/news/just-wanna-rock-mcvertt-jersey-club).
It hasn't slowed down. The flips and remixes on this week's [Rising Now chart](/hot) are spreading the same way, one clip at a time.

title: Why UNIIQU3 Is Called the Queen of Jersey Club
description: UNIIQU3 went from classically trained pianist to touring Jersey club DJ and producer. Her career, her biggest records and how she uses samples.
dek: Newark's UNIIQU3 went from classically trained pianist to a DJ who tours North America, Europe and Asia. Sampling is at the center of how she works.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: [UNIIQU3](/artists/uniiqu3) came up in Newark's club scene in the early 2010s with a background most club DJs don't have: classical piano. She learned production and sampling on a keyboard, and you can hear that musical training in how her tracks are built.

Her 2018 single "Microdosing" was a breakout. The same year she made "Off the Chain" with TT The Artist, produced by Mighty Mark. She has remixed Chloe Bailey and Aluna George, and her Jersey club remix was part of Chloe Bailey's Coachella performance. She has toured with Tinashe, curated the TECHNO IS BLACK playlist on Spotify and plays regularly across North America, Europe and Asia.

In 2024 she appeared in Serato's Hometown Sounds series with Just Blaze and Rah Digga. For it, she flipped Rah Digga's "Party & Bullshit 2003," a Just Blaze production, into a Jersey club track. She works with modern tools like Serato Sample and its stem separation, but the goal is the same as it always was in the club: find the part of a record that gets a room moving.

body.quote: It's just so dope to be behind the decks and have everybody in unison for that one moment.
body.by: UNIIQU3, speaking to The FADER in 2024

body.p: Back in 2014 she described Jersey club as "your morning coffee and your midnight Red Bull." A decade later she is still one of the people making sure that's true. Read more about the roots of the sound in our [history of Jersey club music](/news/history-of-jersey-club-music), or hear where the next generation is taking it on [Rising Now](/hot).

title: Jersey Club in 2026: Labs, Club Noise and Faster Tempos
description: Jersey club keeps changing. Labs, the #ClubNoise sound and 170 to 180 BPM variants, plus the crews and producers pushing the genre forward.
dek: More than 20 years in, Jersey club is less one style than a family of them. These are the traditions and sub-styles moving it forward.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Jersey club started out as Brick City club in Newark in the early 2000s, a local take on the Baltimore club sound. Today it covers several styles that share the same roots.

The foundation hasn't moved much. Bass-heavy 808 triplet drums sit in sync with gun clicks and squeaky bed samples, usually around 130 BPM. Pioneers like [DJ Tameil](/artists/djtameil), whose early releases on his own Anthrax Records label helped set the template, and crews like the Brick Bandits laid it down.

The Brick Bandits also helped start a run of Jersey club supergroups, including Project X, Twerknation28, 4KAE and Anthem Gxds. The current scene includes [UNIIQU3](/artists/uniiqu3), [DJ Sliink](/artists/djsliink), R3LL, Andy pls and MANIIA.
A lab, short for collab, is a track where several producers each make their own section. It suits a scene where everyone has a signature sound and wants it heard.
Tempos keep going up. Newer variants run at 170 to 180 BPM, and a sub-style called #ClubNoise, started by markds, uses distorted 808s and fast, sharp chopping.

body.quote: Jersey Club is that bass you feel in your chest the second it hits.

body.p: You can hear all of this changing week to week. Many of the tracks on the [Rising Now chart](/hot) are flips, remixes and labs uploaded in just the last few weeks. For the backstory, start with our [history of Jersey club music](/news/history-of-jersey-club-music).

title: The Tang Dance, Jersey Drill and the Dance Culture Behind Jersey Club
description: Jersey club was built for dancing. Where the Tang dance came from, how Jersey drill branched off, and how dancers spread the sound worldwide.
dek: Jersey club has always been dance music first. Its dance styles and offshoots are a big part of how it keeps finding new listeners.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: The way to judge a Jersey club record is to watch what it does to a room. The genre came out of Newark in the early 2000s as a local version of Baltimore club, and it was made at 130 to 140 BPM for dancing.
In the mid-2010s a darker branch appeared. Jersey drill brought Chicago drill influences into the club template. It keeps the bounce and changes the mood.

body.h2: Where the Tang dance comes from

body.p: The Tang dance started in Philadelphia and became closely tied to Jersey club. It's built on expressive arm movements that look like boxing or flexing, and dancers often perform it battle-style. It went viral on TikTok in the 2020s and brought the music to people who had never heard of Newark.

The pattern repeats through the genre's history. First the parties, then MySpace, SoundCloud and mix CDs, then video apps. Each wave brought new dancers, and the dancers brought new listeners. That line runs all the way to Lil Uzi Vert's 2022 hit "Just Wanna Rock," produced by Newark's MCVertt. Read [the story behind that record](/news/just-wanna-rock-mcvertt-jersey-club).
To hear what dance floors are moving to right now, check this week's [Rising Now chart](/hot). It tracks the Jersey club uploads gaining the most plays.

title: How MCVertt's Beat for "Just Wanna Rock" Took Jersey Club Mainstream
description: The story of Lil Uzi Vert's "Just Wanna Rock," the Jersey club single co-produced by 19-year-old Newark producer MCVertt, and why it mattered.
dek: Lil Uzi Vert's 2022 single wasn't a rap song or a rock song. It was Jersey club, co-produced by a teenager from Newark.
author: Jersey Club Radio

body.p: Lil Uzi Vert released "Just Wanna Rock" in October 2022 as the lead single from the album that became Pink Tape (2023). By then it already had serious momentum on TikTok, where Uzi had teased it before release.
Stereogum summed it up in one line.

body.quote: Uzi has gone full Jersey club on this one.

body.p: The track runs about two minutes and is driven by rhythm and movement rather than verses. That made it a natural fit for dance videos.
The beat came from Synthetic, who had worked with Yeat, and MCVertt, a 19-year-old Jersey club producer from Newark and a member of Project X, the Jersey collective of producers, dancers and artists.

body.h2: What it did for Jersey club

body.p: "Just Wanna Rock" peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100. By December 2022, Complex counted more than 70 million Spotify streams and 17 million views on the video. It put a Newark production style in front of a mainstream audience that had never heard the name Jersey club, twenty years after the sound first took shape. Our [history of Jersey club music](/news/history-of-jersey-club-music) covers how it got there.
The sound has kept moving since. Hear this week's fastest-rising Jersey club tracks on [Rising Now](/hot).
